text: I used to have the power of when I was school board chair. All right, we're going to get started. Welcome back from lunch, everybody. So I want to welcome everyone to this first meeting of the Housing Committee for 2026, and my first meeting as committee chair, so very grateful for that.

Just a couple things before we move on to presentations. Similar to earlier, I want to first thank Chairman McKay for his faith in me. I know this is a huge priority for the board, and so I'm really honored to be chairing this committee. And a really big thank you to Supervisor Palchuk also for her years of outstanding stewardship leading the housing committee.

As we all have talked about, housing affordability is at the core of many challenges that our community faces today and a huge impact for two reasons and two imperatives. An economic imperative, an economic development imperative to have a wide range of housing so people can live and work here. And a moral imperative grounded in our commitment to One Fairfax.

And so with those two imperatives in mind, I'm really appreciative of the board matter brought by Chairman McKay in 2025 regarding housing initiatives to increase housing production, as well as the 2022 board matter to set a goal of 10,000 affordable housing units. Those are all really, really great initiatives to address our housing issues.

And I'm deeply excited to work on this very fundamental matter. So today we will have two presentations led by our housing director, Tom Fleetwood. And I know he's supporting his work by Deputy Director Anna Shapiro and Director of Real Estate and Community Development Finance, Callie Seltzer.

I hope I said your name right. The first presentation will feature highlights of the recently competed housing needs assessment, which I'm going to anticipate is going to generate a lot of discussion today. And the second presentation will provide updates on the work towards a 10,000-unit affordable housing goal and the work of the interagency staff housing task force.

affordability is a national issue, it's a state issue, and it is especially an acute challenge here in Fairfax County. As the board is aware, housing for all income levels, a healthy housing market is essential to our economic success and affordability, for job creation, retention, and success for low and moderate income families as well. The headline concern here truly is that not addressing the challenges in our market could lead to an out-migration of people and jobs. And that's why

this is so terribly important for our community. Go ahead to the next one. We have essentially two housing markets, one for homeownership and one for rental. And neither of those markets is meeting the needs in our economy, especially for low and moderate income working families.

Fairfax County residents have very high median incomes. Renters have a median income of over $93,000, and owners as of 2023 have a median income of over $178,000. But homeownership today is effectively out of reach for all but those with very high incomes, freezing out young professionals and people who want to move on from renting into homeownership, a population that was identified very clearly in the Chairman's Board matter in

September. So we thought this slide was especially compelling, and it shows job creation versus housing delivery between 2013 and 2023. And as you can see here, Fairfax County has created more than two jobs for every housing unit delivered during that time. And that is as compared to our regional neighbors. And that's a testament both to the desirability of our jurisdiction, the effectiveness of our economic development strategies, but it does highlight

that housing production in the market has not kept up with demand. Turning to the question of the rental market, we have a major gap for households at 60% of the area median income and below. And other than those being delivered through the board's investments and policies, the market is not and will not deliver for low and moderate income households in this community.

To afford Fairfax County's typical market rent of $2,500, a household would need to make at least $100,000 a year. To purchase the median home, you need an income of nearly $230,000 a year. Single workers earning between $50,000 and $70,000 can afford a monthly rent of $1,400 to $2,000 a month. And there's an existing housing shortage for this cohort, meaning they're cost burdened and renting homes beyond their means. Nearly 80% of the households earning 80% of the area median

income and below are cost-burdened, spending over 30% of their incomes on their housing costs. Overall, 45% of all renter households are cost-burdened in Fairfax County. Taking a deeper dive into home ownership, there is truly a widening affordability gap for for-sale housing in our community.

Renters in our economy wanting to make the leap to home ownership have seen the gap between what they can afford and the median house price more than triple between 2010 and 2023. This challenge is compounded by the continuation of a high interest rate environment post-pandemic, which further depresses purchasing power. Rising home prices have deeply constrained purchasing power. As of right now, at 100% of area median income, a household could afford a mortgage of

about $586,000. The median renter household earns about $100,000 a year, but the median sales price in our market, which ranges from about $730,000 to $770,000, is affordable to households earning 140% of median income and above. It's important to note that in 2022, for example, if we can go to that next not that one the next one it's important to note that in 2022 forgive me back to the

previous slide I'm sorry in 2022 for example the median renter household could could afford only about 20 percent of all homes sold next slide that one from 2021 to 2025 only 13 percent of the for sale homes produced were affordable to families earning less than a hundred thousand than 100% of median income, and most of those were likely produced by the board's inclusionary housing policies. More than a third of all new homes during that period sold for more than $1.1

million, including every single family home produced during that period. Buying in Fairfax County requires high levels of upfront cash. 50% of all homes sold from 2022 to 2024 had at least 20% in cash for a down payment. And of those, 20% were all cash transactions. Back to our median renter household, which we think is a very good proxy for, you know, sort of the challenges that

low and moderate income families are facing getting into homeownership, they would have to save for about 15 years to get to a competitive 20% down payment. Now a deeper dive into the rental

With respect, focusing more on the lower-income households and as renters, there is a deep shortage of housing that's affordable for people at 60% and below right now. We have a standing deficit in our market right now of about 13,800 units. And we have 60% and below households that are having to compete for units that are not affordable to them. This affordability mismatch

where lower income renters are renting at higher prices because that's what's available in the market, except for affordable housing we have and are producing. Looking to the future, Fairfax County can expect to need 41,000 to 95,000 new homes across all incomes by 2035. These estimates are broadly in line with what we have in the Comprehensive Plan housing section and are driven
by job and population growth. Based on these estimates, we believe our 2019 work on the need for 15,000 net new units at 60% and below was at least correct and potentially conservative.

And again, that doesn't include the deficit I referred to earlier of nearly $14,000. Looking forward, production must double in Fairfax County in order to reach the low estimate of what we believe will be needed.
And there are a couple of points that I wanted to make here. Between 2014 and 2023, we had 20,000 new homes permitted. During that same period, the board has approved rezonings for 96,000 new units.

So just to give you an idea of what's getting produced versus what you've approved. And I think that's really an important point. Based on the projected need at all income levels, as I said, we must at least double between now and 2035.

And we must continue our path to the 10,000 new affordable units at 60% of AMI and below.
